reading.title: What Holds a Neighborhood Together
reading.purpose: Explore the shared habits, rules, and small actions that turn a group of people into a community.
paras: A street is more than a row of brick homes and sidewalks. People on one block can be very diverse, speaking many tongues, cooking new foods, and working odd hours. Even so, shared daily habits can turn strangers into a true home.

Every strong group relies on norms, the usual ways people are expected to act. Shoveling a neighbor's icy steps or keeping music low at night are simple examples. A shared ritual also helps. This repeated act with special meaning might be a spring tree planting or a warm summer block dinner.

Good blocks grow through mutual trust, a respect felt equally on both sides. When neighbors cooperate to run a book swap or paint a park bench, their collective effort gets much more done than one person working alone. Many residents volunteer on Saturday mornings simply because they care about their street.

Civic life is the shared work of running a town or block. It works best when meetings stay inclusive, welcoming everyone so nobody feels left out. Even after a close vote, fair groups still listen to the minority, the smaller group of voters whose views still count.

No group agrees on every choice. Still, clear norms, kind listening, and willing hands keep the whole block strong. When people feel heard and safe, they gladly pass that same care on to the next family that moves in.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "inclusive" most nearly means
choices: limited to people who have lived on the block for ten years
welcoming everyone so nobody feels left out of the group
focused only on planting street trees and fixing benches
decided quickly without listening to the smaller side
qs.why: Paragraph 4 defines inclusive right after the comma as "welcoming everyone so nobody feels shut out."

qs.q: Which sentence gives everyday examples of neighborhood norms?
choices: A street is more than a row of brick homes and sidewalks.
Shoveling a neighbor's icy steps or keeping music low at night are simple examples.
Many residents volunteer on Saturday mornings simply because they care about their street.
No group agrees on every choice.
qs.why: This sentence provides two concrete examples of unwritten neighborhood expectations.

ev.text: Shoveling a neighbor's icy steps or keeping music low at night are simple examples.

qs.q: Why should a fair block meeting still listen to the minority after a close vote?
choices: Because the smaller group always gets to cancel the next book swap.
Because only the smaller group lives near the painted park benches.
Because their views count and keep everyone included.
Because unwritten norms require every vote to end in a complete tie.
qs.why: Paragraph 4 links inclusive civic life with listening to the minority whose views still count.

qs.q: What is the main idea of this reading?
choices: Shared habits, teamwork, and fair listening build a strong block.
Neighbors should always agree on every single vote at their town meetings.
Summer block dinners are the only way to welcome new residents to a street.
People who speak different tongues rarely share the same brick sidewalks.
qs.why: The passage highlights norms, rituals, mutual trust, cooperation, and inclusive listening as the glue that holds a block together.

clues.text: the usual ways people are expected to act
a respect felt equally on both sides
